solution.concept_anchor: Lokpal trial timeline and property attachment powers

statement_analysis.statement: The Lokpal Act requires that the trial before a Special Court in a Lokpal-referred case must be completed within one year, extendable in six-month blocks with recorded reasons.
statement_analysis.reason: The trial completion target under the Lokpal Act is two years (not one year), extendable in six-month blocks by the Special Court with recorded reasons.

statement_analysis.statement: Lokpal has the power to direct attachment of property of a public servant under investigation, as part of its powers under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
statement_analysis.reason: Lokpal is empowered to direct attachment of property during investigation — a significant preventive power to stop dissipation of proceeds of corruption.

statement_analysis.statement: The investigation wing of Lokpal is an entirely separate body from the CBI and once Lokpal refers a case to the CBI, it cannot also assign the same matter to its own investigation wing.
statement_analysis.reason: While Lokpal has its own Investigation Wing, the Act gives Lokpal discretion in directing cases to either the CBI or its own wing — but there is no statutory bar on Lokpal's oversight continuing regardless of which agency investigates. The framing that referral to CBI bars Lokpal's wing is incorrect.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) identifying only Statement 3 as incorrect tempts students who know the trial timeline is wrong in Statement 1 but are uncertain about Statement 3's fine print.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Trial must be completed within 'one year' — the Act specifies TWO years; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Property attachment power during investigation — confirmed by the Act; Statement 2 IS correct.
Statement 3: Once referred to CBI, Lokpal cannot assign to own wing — this is a fabricated restriction; the Act provides Lokpal discretion; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — answer is (c) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a temporal-swap: substituting 'one year' for the correct 'two years'. Students who remember 'year-based extension blocks' may accept 'one year' as the base period without scrutinising the number. Statement 3 introduces a fabricated restriction that sounds procedurally logical — once you refer to CBI, why would you also use your own wing? This logic-trap catches students who reason from plausibility rather than statutory knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The Lokpal Act's trial and investigation provisions contain specific numerical thresholds that are high-value precision-recall targets.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The trial completion target in Special Courts is two years, not one year. Extensions are permissible in six-month blocks if the Special Court records reasons.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Lokpal has powers under the Prevention of Corruption Act to direct property attachment during investigation — preventing corrupt officials from dissipating assets before trial.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: There is no statutory bar preventing Lokpal from using its own Investigation Wing after referring a matter to CBI or vice versa. Lokpal retains supervisory discretion over referred cases regardless of the investigating agency.

Value Addition:
• Preliminary inquiry: 30 days (extendable to 6 months); Investigation: 6 months (extendable to 1 year); Trial: 2 years (extendable in 6-month blocks).
• Property attachment prevents 'flight of capital' — a critical tool given that corruption often involves offshore accounts and asset concealment.
• The 'two-year trial target' is directory in practice — courts have upheld longer trials without rendering them void.

solution.concept_anchor: Anonymous complaints and complainant eligibility under Lokpal
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) stating that anonymous complaints are permitted if accompanied by supporting documents sounds like a reasonable administrative accommodation, tempting students who reason by analogy with RTI or other regulatory processes.
elimination_logic: Recall the Lokpal Act's provisions on who can file a complaint: any person, society registered under the Societies Registration Act, or trust — complainant must be identifiable.
Anonymous complaints are not directly entertained under the Lokpal Act — the complainant's identity is required for the false complaint penalty mechanism to function.
Eliminate (a): Complaints are not restricted to Indian citizens only — any 'person' can file.
Eliminate (c): No provision permits anonymous complaints even with supporting documents.
Eliminate (d): NGOs can file complaints — they are not excluded.
Confirm (b): The Lokpal Act requires an identified complainant — a person, society, or trust; anonymous complaints are not directly processed.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap adds a plausible condition — 'anonymous complaints with supporting documents' — that sounds like a reasonable exception but does not exist in the Act. The prohibition on anonymous complaints is structurally connected to the false complaint penalty provision: if the complainant is anonymous, there is no person to hold accountable for false filing. Students who reason from administrative pragmatism rather than statutory precision will select option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The Lokpal's complaint mechanism requires an identified complainant — anonymity is not accommodated under the Act.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Act does not restrict complaint-filing to Indian citizens. Any 'person' — including foreign nationals — can approach Lokpal; 'person' is broadly defined.
• Option (b) — Correct: Complaints must be filed by an identified person, a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, or a trust. Anonymous complaints are not directly processed under the Lokpal Act.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: No exception exists for anonymous complaints even if accompanied by documentary evidence. The identity requirement is absolute under the Act.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Registered NGOs (societies and trusts) are explicitly eligible to file complaints — they are not excluded.

Value Addition:
• The identity requirement enables Lokpal to impose penalties for false complaints — a deterrent mechanism that requires a named party.
• Whistleblowers seeking anonymity must approach the Whistleblowers Protection Act, 2014 mechanism — a separate and complementary process.
• The exclusion of anonymous complaints has been criticised as limiting the institution's reach, particularly in matters where the complainant fears retaliation.

solution.concept_anchor: Failed Lokpal Bills count and ARC recommendations

statement_analysis.statement: The First Administrative Reforms Commission that first recommended a Lokpal for India was chaired by Morarji Desai.
statement_analysis.reason: The First ARC, which recommended an Ombudsman (Lokpal) for India in 1966, was initially chaired by Morarji Desai — later chaired by K. Hanumanthaiah after Desai became Deputy PM.

statement_analysis.statement: Before the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 was finally passed, exactly ten Lokpal Bills had been introduced in Parliament and had lapsed.
statement_analysis.reason: Eight Lokpal Bills were introduced and lapsed between 1968 and 2011 — not ten. The 2011 Bill (the ninth attempt) preceded the successful 2013 Act.

statement_analysis.statement: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2005-2009) recommended establishment of a model Lokayukta to bring uniformity across states.
statement_analysis.reason: The Second ARC under Veerappa Moily did recommend a model Lokayukta for all states — though this recommendation was never implemented and states retain wide variation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Anna Hazare movement of 2011 specifically demanded that the Lokpal Bill should give the institution power to investigate sitting judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Jan Lokpal Bill demanded a stronger and more independent Lokpal, bringing judges under Lokpal directly was not the central demand — the key dispute was over the independence of the institution, its composition, and CBI superintendence, not specifically about including SC/HC judges.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Only two' is the distractor for students who wrongly accept Statement 2 (10 bills) and Statement 4 (judges demand) as correct, leaving only Statements 1 and 3 as wrong.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: First ARC chaired by Morarji Desai — this is correct (initially; he became Deputy PM and Hanumanthaiah continued); Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: 'Exactly ten bills lapsed' — the historically established figure is eight bills (1968-2011); Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Second ARC recommended model Lokayukta — confirmed in ARC reports; Statement 3 is correct.

Statement 4: Anna Hazare movement demanded SC/HC judges be covered — this was not the central demand of the 2011 movement; judiciary inclusion was a peripheral issue, not the defining demand; Statement 4 is incorrect.
Two statements correct (1 and 3) — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses plausible-fabrication with a number close to the correct figure (10 vs. 8). Students who know 'many bills failed' but haven't memorised the exact count accept 10 as plausible. Statement 4 uses a half-true claim — the judiciary was discussed during the Anna Hazare agitation but including SC/HC judges under Lokpal directly was not the central demand of the movement. These two fabricated-truth options flank the two genuine facts.
solution.final_explanation:
The legislative history of the Lokpal is a series of failed attempts spanning nearly five decades.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The First ARC was chaired by Morarji Desai (who later became Deputy PM, with K. Hanumanthaiah completing the chairmanship). The 1966 recommendation for an Ombudsman was the genesis of the Lokpal concept in India.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Eight Lokpal Bills were introduced and lapsed between 1968 and 2011 — not ten. The ninth attempt (2011 Bill) contributed to the eventual successful passage of the 2013 Act.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Second ARC (2005-2009) under Veerappa Moily recommended a model Lokayukta Act for all states to bring uniformity — a recommendation that remains unimplemented.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Anna Hazare movement's core demands were institutional independence, broad jurisdiction over political executives, and control over CBI. Specifically including sitting SC/HC judges was not the defining demand of the 2011 agitation.

Value Addition:
• First Lokpal Bill was introduced in 1968 — four years after the Santhanam Committee (1962-64) on corruption.
• The Jan Lokpal Bill (civil society version) vs. Government's Lokpal Bill differed primarily on: CBI superintendence, jurisdiction over PM, and selection committee composition.
• 8 failed bills is a standard UPSC exam fact — test-takers should memorise this number precisely.

solution.concept_anchor: India Lokpal hybrid design vs. ICAC and Swedish models

statement_analysis.statement: India deliberately separated the investigation function (assigned to CBI/Lokpal Investigation Wing) from the adjudicatory function (retained by Lokpal) in order to avoid the concentration of power seen in bodies like the Hong Kong ICAC.
statement_analysis.reason: The Indian design consciously avoided giving Lokpal integrated investigative-prosecutorial-judicial powers — the ICAC model's power concentration was cited as a concern, leading India to keep investigation with a separate agency while Lokpal retains adjudicatory oversight.

statement_analysis.statement: The Swedish Ombudsman, which is the world's oldest Ombudsman institution, investigates complaints filed only through referral by members of the Swedish Parliament, similar to the UK Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration.
statement_analysis.reason: The Swedish Ombudsman (JO) accepts direct complaints from citizens — it does not require parliamentary referral. It is the UK Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration that investigates only through MP referral. This is a fundamental institutional difference between the two models.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) accepting both statements as correct tempts students who have surface knowledge of Ombudsman models and conflate the Swedish and UK referral mechanisms.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: India's design separated investigation from adjudication to avoid ICAC-style power concentration — this is documented in legislative debates and UPSC-relevant comparative analysis; Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: Swedish Ombudsman requires parliamentary referral like the UK Commissioner — this is incorrect; Sweden's JO accepts direct citizen complaints; only the UK Commissioner uses the MP referral route; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the UK Parliamentary Commissioner's MP-referral mechanism with the Swedish Ombudsman's direct-access model. Students learn that both are European, non-prosecutorial Ombudsman institutions and conflate their access mechanisms. The Swedish JO is notable precisely for being the world's oldest Ombudsman and for accepting direct citizen complaints — making it a model of accessibility, unlike the UK system which filters complaints through elected representatives.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparative Ombudsman models are a niche but tested area, especially in the context of India's institutional design choices.

• Statement 1 — Correct: India's Lokpal deliberately separates investigation (CBI/Investigation Wing) from adjudication (Lokpal itself) — a design choice informed by concerns about power concentration in integrated models like Hong Kong's ICAC.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Swedish Ombudsman (JO — Justitieombudsman, established 1809) is directly accessible by all citizens — no parliamentary filter is required. It is the UK Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration that can be approached only through a Member of Parliament. Attributing the referral requirement to Sweden is a factual error.

Value Addition:
• Sweden's JO was established in 1809 — making it 214+ years old and the template for all subsequent Ombudsman institutions globally.
• The ICAC (Independent Commission Against Corruption) model has been influential in Asia — Singapore, Malaysia, and Hong Kong all have variants.
• India's Lokpal remains a 'hybrid' — it has quasi-judicial powers (unlike pure advisory models) but lacks suo motu powers (unlike proactive investigative bodies).

solution.concept_anchor: LoP absence and Lokpal appointment controversy
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) stating appointments cannot proceed without a formally recognised LoP mirrors the initial controversy and the early political arguments — students unaware of the SC's 2018 resolution may select this.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a Lok Sabha with no formally recognised Leader of Opposition — a situation that occurred in the 16th and 17th Lok Sabhas.

The Supreme Court, in 2018, addressed this issue and ruled that the Lokpal appointment process could proceed with the leader of the single largest opposition party participating in lieu of the formal LoP.
Eliminate (a): Indefinite postponement without LoP is not legally mandated — SC cleared the path for appointments.
Eliminate (b): Appointment without a formal LoP is permissible with leader of single largest party as substitute.
Eliminate (c): There is no constitutional provision or Lokpal Act provision that shifts LoP's role to the Rajya Sabha Chairman.
Confirm (d): The SC held that the leader of the single largest opposition party can participate in the Selection Committee in lieu of the formal LoP — process can proceed.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates through option (c), which substitutes the Rajya Sabha Chairman as the replacement for LoP. This sounds procedurally logical — the Chairman presides over the Upper House and has some constitutional standing — but has no basis in the Lokpal Act or the SC ruling. The actual resolution involved the leader of the single largest opposition party in the Lok Sabha, not any Rajya Sabha figure. Students familiar with the controversy but uncertain about the SC's specific resolution may gravitate toward the plausible-but-wrong substitution.
solution.final_explanation:
The absence of a formally recognised Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha created a constitutional controversy about whether Lokpal appointments could proceed — resolved by the Supreme Court.

Applicable principle: When no formal Leader of Opposition exists in the Lok Sabha (because no single opposition party holds the required 10% of seats), the Supreme Court held in 2018 that the leader of the single largest opposition party could participate in the Selection Committee in that capacity. The process need not be stalled.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The SC did not indefinitely stay the process — it provided a workable solution.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The SC explicitly ruled that appointments could proceed without a formal LoP, using the largest opposition party leader as a substitute.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: No provision or judicial ruling designates the Rajya Sabha Chairman as a substitute for the LoP in Lokpal's Selection Committee.
• Option (d) — Correct: The SC's 2018 ruling established that the leader of the single largest opposition party can fill the LoP slot in the Selection Committee — enabling appointment despite the structural gap.

Value Addition:
• The 10% seat threshold for formal LoP recognition comes from the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977.
• First Lokpal Justice P.C. Ghose was appointed under exactly this arrangement in March 2019.
• This constitutional controversy exposed a lacuna in the Lokpal Act's drafting — later amendments sought to address it.

solution.concept_anchor: CVC advisory nature, Lokpal prosecutorial power, and jurisdictional scope

statement_analysis.statement: The Central Vigilance Commission can only recommend action — it lacks the authority to directly sanction prosecution or exercise quasi-judicial powers, unlike the Lokpal.
statement_analysis.reason: CVC is an advisory and recommendatory body; it cannot sanction prosecution or exercise quasi-judicial adjudicatory functions. Lokpal, by contrast, is the sanctioning authority for prosecution of Group A officers and has quasi-judicial powers.

statement_analysis.statement: The CVC's jurisdiction is limited to vigilance matters concerning Group A officers and above, while the Lokpal's jurisdiction additionally extends to political executives — the Prime Minister, Union Ministers, and Members of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: CVC covers vigilance matters for Group A and above in the central services — it does not cover political executives. Lokpal explicitly covers PM, Union Ministers, and MPs (with specified conditions), making its jurisdictional scope qualitatively broader.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the CVC and the Lokpal were established as statutory bodies through Acts of Parliament passed in the same year.
statement_analysis.reason: The CVC was established by the CVC Act, 2003; the Lokpal was established by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 — they were created a decade apart, not in the same year.

solution.strong_distractor: d — All three correct tempts students who recognise Statements 1 and 2 as accurate but are not precise about the CVC Act's year (2003) vs. Lokpal Act (2013).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: CVC advisory only, Lokpal has quasi-judicial/prosecutorial powers — this is a core institutional distinction; Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: CVC covers Group A+, Lokpal additionally covers PM, Ministers, MPs — confirmed jurisdictional difference; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3: Both established in the same year — CVC Act 2003, Lokpal Act 2013 — different years; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — answer is (a) 1 and 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a partial-truth: both CVC and Lokpal are statutory bodies (true) created by Acts of Parliament (true) — but the 'same year' claim is false. Students who remember both are statutory and Parliament-created but haven't memorised the precise years accept Statement 3. The decade gap (2003 vs. 2013) is a precision fact that distinguishes thorough preparation from surface knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The CVC and Lokpal occupy different tiers in India's anti-corruption architecture — advisory/administrative vs. quasi-judicial/political.

• Statement 1 — Correct: CVC can recommend but cannot compel action or adjudicate. Lokpal has prosecutorial teeth — it sanctions prosecution and has quasi-judicial powers, making it institutionally stronger.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CVC's remit is administrative vigilance for senior civil servants (Group A and above). Lokpal's reach extends to the entire political executive — PM (with conditions), Union Ministers, and MPs — a qualitatively different and politically sensitive jurisdiction.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: CVC was created by the CVC Act, 2003; Lokpal by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. They were enacted a full decade apart.

Value Addition:
• Before the CVC Act, 2003, CVC existed only through an executive resolution of 1964 — statutory backing came 39 years later.
• CVC's recommendatory findings go to the disciplinary authority, which may or may not act — a structural accountability gap.
• Lokpal's power to directly sanction prosecution for Group A officers was the most significant reform in the 2013 Act.

solution.concept_anchor: Lokpal jurisdiction categories and their specific coverage conditions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) incorrectly pairs 'Group C/D officers' with 'excluded from Lokpal jurisdiction', which some students believe because they associate Lokpal with senior officials only.
elimination_logic: List I item A (Group C and D officers of Central Government): Lokpal covers all Groups A/B/C/D — matches List II item 3 (fully within jurisdiction, subject to prescribed procedures).
List I item B (NGOs receiving foreign/government donations above threshold): Covered as part of the expanded definition of covered entities — matches List II item 1.

List I item D (Central Government employees on deputation to state governments): Not excluded by deputation — central employment status determines Lokpal's jurisdiction, not current posting location — matches List II item 2.
Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap is embedded in item D: central employees on deputation to state governments. Students reason that since the employee is functionally working under a state government, they fall outside Lokpal's jurisdiction. But the Lokpal Act's jurisdiction is based on the nature of employment (central public servant) not the location or entity of deployment. A central officer on state deputation remains a central public servant under Lokpal's jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
Lokpal's jurisdictional boundaries are determined by the nature of the public servant's central employment, not by their current deployment location or functional role.

Correct pairings:
• A (Group C and D officers) — 3: All four Groups of central government employees are within Lokpal's jurisdiction — the Act does not limit coverage to senior officers only.
• B (NGOs receiving above-threshold foreign/government donations) — 1: Such organisations are explicitly brought within Lokpal's coverage — a significant expansion of the accountability net.
• C (HC and SC judges) — 4: Judges are excluded from Lokpal's jurisdiction and remain subject to the Supreme Court's in-house procedure for accountability.
• D (Central employees on state deputation) — 2: Deputation to a state government does not remove a central public servant from Lokpal's jurisdiction — central employment status governs, not deployment location.

Value Addition:
• The inclusion of NGOs represents a recognition that corruption can involve entities receiving public funds even if not formal government bodies.
• The in-house procedure for judges was established by the Supreme Court in K. Veeraswami vs. Union of India (1991) and subsequent Full Court resolutions.
• An employee of a body substantially financed by the Central Government is also within Lokpal's jurisdiction — even without direct employment.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronology of anti-corruption legislative milestones in India
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) placing the CVC Act before the RTI Act but after the PC Act in incorrect order tempts students who know the rough sequencing but misplace CVC Act (2003) relative to RTI (2005).
elimination_logic: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 — enacted during Rajiv Gandhi government; this is the oldest in the list.
CVC Act, 2003 — gave statutory backing to Central Vigilance Commission; predates RTI by 2 years.
RTI Act, 2005 — landmark transparency legislation; comes after CVC Act.
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 — the most recent; comes last in this sequence.
Correct sequence: PC Act (1988) → CVC Act (2003) → RTI Act (2005) → Lokpal Act (2013) — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the CVC Act (2003) vs. RTI Act (2005) sequencing — both are early 2000s statutes that students sometimes reverse. The Prevention of Corruption Act (1988) is the anchor — no confusion there. But students who associate the 'transparency movement' with the general 2000s reform era may place RTI before CVC Act. The two-year gap (2003 vs. 2005) is the precision point that separates prepared from unprepared students.
solution.final_explanation:
India's anti-corruption legislative architecture evolved through distinct legislative landmarks over 25 years.

Correct sequence:
1. Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 — replaced the 1947 Act; defined 'public servant', criminal misconduct, trap cases, and the prosecution sanction requirement.
2. CVC Act, 2003 — gave statutory backing to the Central Vigilance Commission (previously only an executive resolution body since 1964).
3. RTI Act, 2005 — established citizens' right to access government information; a transparency tool that complements anti-corruption mechanisms.
4. Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 — established Lokpal as a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman; the most recent and institutionally comprehensive piece.

Each wrong option either reverses the CVC/RTI sequence or misplaces the PC Act.

Value Addition:
• The PC Act, 1988 itself was amended significantly in 2018 — adding bribe-giver liability and extending sanction requirements to retired officers.
• CVC was first created by executive resolution in 1964 on the Santhanam Committee's recommendations.
• The 2018 PC Act amendment is considered the most significant update to India's anti-corruption criminal law in three decades.

solution.concept_anchor: PM inquiry threshold — full bench and two-thirds majority requirement

statement_analysis.statement: For Lokpal to proceed with an inquiry against the Prime Minister, a simple majority of the Lokpal's members present and voting must approve the initiation of proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: A simple majority is not sufficient — the Act requires the full bench to sit (all members) and a two-thirds majority of all members to approve proceeding against the PM.

statement_analysis.statement: The Lokpal Act explicitly lists matters relating to international relations, external security, internal security, public order, atomic energy, and space as domains in which the PM cannot be investigated by Lokpal.
statement_analysis.reason: These six categories are the exact statutory exclusions listed in the Act for PM-related complaints — Lokpal has no jurisdiction in these subject matter domains for PM complaints.

statement_analysis.statement: If the Lokpal bench hearing a complaint against the Prime Minister finds no case to proceed, the records of the inquiry must be made public to ensure transparency and deter political misuse of the process.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act mandates the opposite — if no case is found, all records of the PM inquiry must be destroyed, not made public. Public disclosure is prohibited to prevent misuse of inconclusive findings.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) identifying only Statement 3 as incorrect tempts students who correctly flag Statement 3's error but miss that Statement 1 uses 'simple majority' instead of the required two-thirds majority.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Simple majority to proceed against PM — the Act requires full bench + two-thirds majority, not simple majority; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: The six listed exclusions (international relations, security, public order, atomic energy, space) — confirmed by the Act; Statement 2 IS correct.
Statement 3: Records made public if no case found — the Act requires destruction, not disclosure; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — answer is (c) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a scope-extension trap: 'simple majority' sounds procedurally reasonable for institutional decisions, but the PM's special position requires a much higher threshold — full bench + two-thirds. Students who know 'majority approval is needed' but haven't memorised the specific threshold type accept 'simple majority'. Statement 3 inverts the correct provision: public disclosure (transparency logic) sounds right but the Act deliberately mandates destruction to protect the PM from political fallout from inconclusive inquiries.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural thresholds for PM inquiries are among the Act's most distinctive — and most examination-tested — features.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Simple majority is insufficient. The full bench of Lokpal (all members) must convene and a two-thirds majority of all members (not just those present) must approve proceeding against the PM. This is an extraordinary institutional threshold.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Act enumerates six subject matter exclusions for PM complaints: international relations, external security, internal security, public order, atomic energy, and space. These are exhaustive, not illustrative.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Act mandates destruction — not public disclosure — of all inquiry records if Lokpal finds no case against the PM. This reverses the transparency logic to protect the PM from inconclusive inquiry records being weaponised politically.

Value Addition:
• The combination of full bench + two-thirds majority + in camera + records destruction makes PM inquiries effectively the most protected proceedings in the Lokpal framework.
• 'Two-thirds of all members' (not two-thirds of quorum) means even absent members count against the approval threshold — a near-unanimity requirement in practice.
• These protections have been criticised as making the PM investigation provision more symbolic than operational.
